The exclusion was correct for the three repos it was written against and wrong for the four it was applied to, so THE FASTEST SUITES IN THE ESTATE WERE THE ONES NOT BEING RUN. An exclusion written against one repo class and applied to all of them

Two findings were nearly reported from tool output that was itself wrong. A conventional-commit audit measured 12% violations in tabsii-platform using a regex that rejected `feat(db,api):` -- commas are legal in a scope, so the tool was wrong and the repo was fine. Separately, `biffo.sh check release-subject` printed 'No base ref' and looked like a fail-open until its exit code was read properly: it exits 2, loudly. Both would have produced a scoreboard row asserting a defect that does not exist

A cadence step could not be created AT ALL: crm_cadence_steps.brand_id is NOT NULL (denormalised for RLS) and the sibling never supplied it. Every test for the feature constructed a CadenceStep OBJECT — and a Python constructor makes you pass brand_id, so all of them did. Nothing exercised the HTTP path, which is the only place the omission exists. Unit suites green on both sides of the boundary; the feature could not create a step

Every compiled cadence email step FAILED AT DISPATCH: the email action declares `from` required with no default, and the step builder hardcoded to/subject/body without it. Invisible everywhere before a real send — the compile reports success, the definition looks correct in the database, and the failure exists only inside the orchestrator past EventBridge. Only a live capture surfaced it

A merged PR ASSERTED a verification nobody performed. #323 built POST /leads/{id}/status and its description said 'the CRM is pointed here'. It was not — the drawer still sent status through the generic PUT, so the fix existed in Core and nothing in the product used it, and #320 was closed while the failure it described still happened. Caught only by checking which endpoint the deployed UI actually calls before testing

RLS hardening blocked the write path it was designed to permit. Module 052 gave lead_cadence_enrolments a SELECT policy and no others so a caller could not desynchronise it from its scheduled runs; RLS applies to the ENDPOINT's session too, so the transition matched zero rows and converting a lead 500'd with StaleDataError — leaving the cadence armed. The logic was tested thoroughly on SQLite, WHICH HAS NO POLICIES, so every one of those tests ran against a session that could write anything

A deploy-watcher matched 'the newest run named Deploy' without pinning the commit SHA, and reported success for the PREVIOUS commit's deploy — the new one had not been created yet, by one second. Nearly produced a fabricated defect report ('the fix does not work on dev') from a green signal about the wrong artifact. Earlier watchers in the same session DID pin the SHA; the inconsistency was the bug

An approved implementation plan specified a mechanism that CANNOT work: cadence steps were to trigger on lead.captured with a synthetic cadence_id in trigger_filter, but trigger_filter is an exact match over the event payload and lead.captured carries no cadence_id. Every compiled step would have been silently inert; dropping the filter instead makes two active cadences both fire for one lead. Caught by reading _matches_trigger_filter BEFORE building, not after

Resolving an append-only corpus conflict with a regex that assumed BOTH sides had content: this conflict had an EMPTY HEAD side, so the resolver matched nothing and printed '0 conflicts resolved', which was read as 'no conflicts'. Raw conflict markers were committed and pushed into evidence.jsonl. The JSON validation in the same command DID catch it -- and the push ran anyway, because it was chained on the same shell line rather than gated on the validation's exit status. A check that reports without blocking, against the corpus that records that exact failure class

scripts/protection-audit.sh, written specifically to catch a permanently-skipped security gate, was itself fail-open on its first run. It read only stdout and matched with `case`; `gh api` prints its 404 body TO STDOUT for an unprotected branch, so three genuinely unprotected branches fell through to the wildcard and were reported `ok ... {"message":"Branch not protected"} required checks`, exit 0. Found by reading every line of the output rather than the summary

Issue #643 family 5 asked the template to 'make the app DB role name a variable'. It ALREADY WAS -- var.app_db_user existed at core-v0.127.0, added before the issue was filed -- and the second half (make the secret RESOURCE name a variable) is impossible: HCL resource labels are not interpolatable. Both sides already set an identical name, so only the Terraform state address differs and a `moved` block resolves it with no destroy, contradicting the instance's claim that adopting would recreate a live credential. An issue's premise going stale between filing and scheduling, on a claim nobody re-checked

The deployed Core Lambda package contains 1,643 .py files and ZERO .pyc, and /var/task is read-only so the bytecode cache can never be written. deploy-app.yml deletes __pycache__ deliberately, as 'build-time dead weight', to fit an upload size cap. Precompiling takes import 4105ms -> 1575ms at calibrated CPU: a build step added for a size limit silently became ~60% of every cold start, and set the floor under every timeout in the estate. No gate could see it because the artifact was never profiled -- only the source was

Issue #695 asserts build_core_crud_router() returns zero routes on a second call because 'the first call consumes the registry'. Could not be reproduced from two independent directions: the agent writing the #668 guard called it three times against an opted-in model and got identical non-empty sets, and four attempts here returned the SAME count on calls 1/2/3 (never populated-then-empty), with a validation warning firing identically on all three -- which alone disproves consumption. The likely real cause is that app.routes is not flat on FastAPI 0.138: include_router leaves an _IncludedRouter placeholder with no .path, so the idiom the issue quotes reads zero usable routes without anything being consumed. A property of the reader, not the function

The 'Where the work actually lands' table -- headed 'Generated, not typed' and explicitly warning that hand-typed counts go stale -- was itself stale by a factor of 2.5: it read 99 corpus rows and 68 for biffo-template while the corpus held 248 and 126. Three sessions rewrote it in one day (200 -> 99 -> 248) because the figures are transcribed by hand from a generated report, and concurrent sessions cannot converge on a hand-copied number. A generator emitting the markdown directly does not exist

RECURRENCE, third instance in one session, and the class is 'the instrument was the defect'. integrationHealth.redMinutes measured failure-to-recovery wall-clock, so a branch left red at 11:47 and green at 06:36 next morning scored 21.1h -- 89% of it overnight with ZERO pushes against it. Nobody was blocked; everyone was asleep. That number ranked FIRST of five findings on the standup's first real run, and metrics.md instructed the reader to MULTIPLY it by concurrency. The genuinely blocked window was 2.3h, which ranks the finding last. The estate had already established the distinction one metric over, for the runner fleet -- 'flat queue under an idle fleet is not contention' -- and never applied it here

RECURRENCE of 'suspect the ruler', and I was the one who did it: I diagnosed an exit-status bug in practices-daily.sh from a theory, asserted it twice as fact, and built a worktree to fix it. There was no bug. The 'exit 1' came from my own `| head -22`, which SIGPIPEs the script and makes PIPESTATUS[0] report 141; the proposed mechanism was wrong too, since a trailing `if` with a false condition exits 0 in bash. Cost was not the wrong theory but the confidence: it was repeated in two summaries before anyone ran the script without a pipe. The honest residue was real -- the log had no terminal marker, so a truncated run and a complete one were indistinguishable, which is what made the misreading possible

The tool built to find fail-open shipped one, and failed its own test within six minutes of merging. practices-standup.mjs read docs/practices/data/ from wherever it ran; the primary checkout carries only what was merged to dev, and today's snapshot lives on chore/practices-snapshots which is deliberately never merged. Run with default arguments it printed a confident, fully formatted ranking of a TWO-DAY-OLD snapshot with no warning. Worse here than in most places: the output's whole purpose is to direct a day's effort, so it does not merely fail to help, it spends the budget on an old problem and reports success

The 04:30 practices cron 401'd on all fifteen repos and still wrote a well-formed 9.5KB snapshot -- every repo `unmeasured`, estate.merges 0 -- then stopped before rendering, so the bookmarked dashboard silently served the previous day. gh stores its token in the GNOME keyring and hosts.yml carries no oauth_token, so cron has no session D-Bus to read it through. Same class as the ssh-agent gap the script already compensated for twenty lines above: a credential that exists only inside a desktop session. Graceful degradation was right for one unreadable repo and wrong for all of them -- 'nothing could be measured' is not an observation, it is a broken job

Upstream API errors reach the UI as double-encoded JSON because the proxy passes the whole response body as its detail string. core_client.py raises CoreApiError(status, response.text) on every verb, and the routers pass that into HTTPException(detail=...), so FastAPI serialises an already-JSON string a second time: users see {"detail":"{\"detail\":\"Method Not Allowed\"}"}. Pre-existing and general -- every proxied router in the sibling has it -- and invisible until a panel rendered the failure text inline instead of swallowing it

`enforce_admins: false` on ELEVEN of twelve estate repos makes every branch-protection rule advisory for the only human who merges, and no audit reports it. Found because a new stale-merge metric flagged merges in repos carrying `strict: true` -- tabsii-intake, tabsii-geo, biffo-plugin-ideation -- which the gate makes impossible by construction. The explanation is that protection does not bind an admin anywhere except biffo-template, the single repo where `enforce_admins` is on. The daily estate audit checks that branches ARE protected (19 branches, all protected, reported OK every day) and never checks that the protection BINDS anyone, so a repo can show a full required-check list, pass the audit, and still be one where any of it can be walked past without a trace. Two consequences beyond the obvious: H3’s comparator tabsii-crm is NOT gated the same way as its treatment repo biffo-template, a confound the experiment never recorded; and tabsii-platform, added to H3’s treatment arm on 2026-07-31, is also unbound. Nothing was looking -- this surfaced only because an unrelated metric disagreed with a setting
surfacedIn: estate-wide (11 of 12 repos); found via staleMergeShare disagreeing with `strict: true`
fixesIn: not fixed -- extend the daily protection audit to report `enforce_admins`, then decide per repo whether admin bypass is intended

summary: A dead runner and a rejected change were the same number, so an integration branch read as broken when nothing was. `FAILING_CONCLUSIONS` excludes `cancelled` on the stated grounds that a superseded run is not a defect -- correct, and only half the cases: a runner killed mid-job reports `cancelled` only SOMETIMES. The rest of the time GitHub concludes the run `failure` with no failing step, and that label was counted as if code had broken. On tabsii-platform, ALL SIX dev failures inspected had zero failing steps and 3-21 steps left incomplete; one deploy succeeded through thirteen steps and froze on "Package and deploy Lambda". The board read 8 integration failures and 111.7 red minutes on a branch where not one gate had rejected anything. It was invisible because the run-level conclusion is the only thing anyone reads -- diagnosing it needs the per-run jobs payload, which the collector already fetches for another metric entirely. Correcting it: tabsii-platform 24h went 8 failures/111.7 red minutes to 1/0, while biffo-template stayed at 2/54.7 because its failures are genuine -- the fix did not flatter the arm its author had an interest in
surfacedIn: tabsii-platform dev (found while diagnosing rank 4 of the daily standup)
fixesIn: biffo-template scripts/practices-metrics.mjs -- isRunnerKill(), validated against 7 real runs including a negative control

summary: A fix for a mislabelled failure caught one of the two signatures the same fault produces, and looked complete because the cases it was validated against all had the other one. #982 re-attributed runner kills by requiring a step still executing (conclusion null) -- true of all six tabsii-platform runs it was built and validated against. A dying runner also produces a second signature: the stopping step reads `cancelled` and every later step `skipped`, while the RUN still concludes `failure`. Two biffo-platform CI runs died that way, 64 seconds in, and stayed counted as broken code. Found only by diagnosing a different repo a day later. The generalisable trap is that a validation set drawn entirely from one repo shares that repo failure mode, so 7/7 real runs passing proved the rule worked on the shape it was derived from and said nothing about the shape it had never seen. Guarding against laundering a genuine cancellation is structural rather than heuristic: a real cancellation, by hand or by cancel-in-progress, concludes the RUN `cancelled`, which is already excluded before the classifier is reached
surfacedIn: biffo-platform dev (found while diagnosing an unrelated red branch)
fixesIn: biffo-template scripts/practices-metrics.mjs -- STOPPED_SHORT covers both signatures; validated against 16 real runs across 3 repos including 7 negative controls
